Adrian Edin    Michel Kieffer Affiliation: Mikael Johansson, , and Zheng Chen,
Abstract

The communication bottleneck in federated learning (FL) has spurred extensive research into techniques to reduce the volume of data exchanged between client devices and the central parameter server. In this paper, we systematically classify gradient and model compression schemes into three categories based on the type of correlations they exploit: structural, temporal, and spatial. We examine the sources of such correlations, propose quantitative metrics for measuring their magnitude, and reinterpret existing compression methods through this unified correlation-based framework. Our experimental studies demonstrate that the degrees of structural, temporal, and spatial correlations vary significantly depending on task complexity, model architecture, and algorithmic configurations. These findings suggest that algorithm designers should carefully evaluate correlation assumptions under specific deployment scenarios rather than assuming that they are always present. Motivated by these findings, we propose two adaptive compression designs that actively switch between different compression modes based on the measured correlation strength, and we evaluate their performance gains relative to conventional non-adaptive approaches. In summary, our unified taxonomy provides a clean and principled foundation for developing more effective and application-specific compression techniques for FL systems.

Index Terms:
Federated learning, communication efficiency, compression, correlation.

I Introduction

As machine learning (ML)models grow in scale and complexity, training them on massive datasets with a single machine becomes increasingly demanding. The rise of edge computing and data parallelism has driven the emergence of collaborative machine learning, where multiple nodes—each with access to a portion of the data—collaborate to train a shared model without sharing raw samples. This can be done in a network with a master–worker architecture, such as federated learning (FL), or in a decentralized topology with local interactions, such as decentralized learning. In server-based FL, multiple clients iteratively update their local copy of the global model using their own private data. These model updates are then sent to a central parameter server (PS), which aggregates them to obtain an updated global model. Compared to centralized learning, FLoffers advantages such as improved scalability and enhanced data privacy. However, FLalso faces the challenge of a communication bottleneck due to frequent information exchange between local clients and the PS, especially when the exchanged information contains high-dimensional parameter vectors from deep neural networks.

To address this communication bottleneck, several strategies for improving the communication efficiency of FLhave been proposed based on

  • •

    reducing the number of bits transmitted from clients to the server in each communication round, e.g., through model update compression [22];

  • •

    reducing the number of active communication links, e.g., via client selection [10, 21] or event-triggered communication [8, 49];

  • •

    reducing the frequency of communication, e.g., by performing multiple gradient steps before aggregation [43].

In earlier studies, commonly used compression techniques in FL, such as quantization [4] and random sparsification [48], treat the model updates generated by local clients as independent information sources. However, the correlation and redundancy among local model updates can be exploited to achieve more efficient compression. These correlations may arise from the model architecture, the learning algorithm, or other design choices in the FLsystem [47, 46, 6, 37]. Classical coding theory shows that correlated sources can be compressed more efficiently, with greater savings as correlation increases [42]. For instance, in the lossy compression of parallel Gaussian sources, correlation enables lower transmission rates for a given distortion level compared to uncorrelated sources. Another example is predictive coding, widely used in image and video compression, that exploits redundancy between adjacent pixels or consecutive frames to enhance compression efficiency. Inspired by this principle, recent works in FL [52, 12, 2] apply predictive techniques to compress temporally correlated model updates. By forecasting future updates from past ones, only the residuals—representing deviations from the prediction—need to be transmitted, significantly reducing communication overhead when consecutive updates are sufficiently correlated. So far, predictive coding has mainly been applied to exploit temporal correlations in local model updates, but the underlying principle is not limited to the time domain. In fact, similar strategies could also be applied to capture structural correlations within the model itself or spatial correlations across clients, for example, using subspace projection methods [36, 54, 16]. However, whether such correlations are present in practical FLsettings and how they might be effectively measured and leveraged for compression remains an open question. Given the growing interest in redundancy-based compression schemes in the FLliterature, we find it pertinent to examine whether such correlations are observable in practice, and to what extent they can actually contribute to improving communication efficiency.

Our paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We introduce a unified framework for analyzing structural, temporal, and spatial correlations in FL, and propose metrics for measuring each type of correlation.

  • •

    We reinterpret existing redundancy-based compression techniques through the lens of these correlations, offering a new perspective on their underlying design principles.

  • •

    The practical limitations of correlation-based subspace projection methods, such as computational complexity and memory overhead, are also discussed to provide a thorough assessment of their advantages and disadvantages.

  • •

    Based on existing non-adaptive compression schemes, we propose two adaptive designs that measure the strength of correlations on the fly and dynamically switch between different compression modes.

  • •

    We conduct experiments demonstrating that correlation strength varies with model size, task complexity, and system configuration. These results highlight the importance of adaptive compression designs compared to their static counterparts.

II Three Sources of Correlation in Federated Learning

In a FLsystem, a set of KK distributed clients collaborates in training a shared MLmodel under the coordination of a central PS. Each client k∈[K]k\in[K] has local access to subset 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} of the complete dataset 𝒟=∪k=1K𝒟k\mathcal{D}=\cup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}_{k}. The training objective is to minimize a global loss

f⁡(𝒙)=∑k=1Kwk​fk​(𝒙),\displaystyle f({\bm{x}})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}f_{k}({\bm{x}}), (1)

where 𝒙∈ℝd{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the vector of model parameters, wk=|𝒟k|/|𝒟|w_{k}=|\mathcal{D}_{k}|/|\mathcal{D}| are aggregation weights proportional to the amount of data held by client kk, fk​(𝒙)=1|𝒟k|​∑ξ∈𝒟kℓ⁡(𝒙,ξ)f_{k}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{k}|}\sum_{\xi\in\mathcal{D}_{k}}\ell({\bm{x}};\xi) is the local objective of client kk, and ℓ⁡(𝒙,ξ)\ell({\bm{x}};\xi) is the loss for sample ξ\xi. A canonical FLalgorithm is federated averaging (FedAvg) [33], which proceeds iteratively as follows:

  1. 1.

    The PSbroadcasts the current global model parameters 𝒙(t){\bm{x}}^{(t)} to all clients.

  2. 2.

    Each client kk performs τ\tau local stochastic gradient updates using mini-batches

    𝒙k(t,i+1)=𝒙k(t,i)−γ∇fk(𝒙k(t,i),𝒟k(t,i)),i=0,…,τ−1,\mkern-3.0mu{\bm{x}}_{k}^{(t,i+1)}={\bm{x}}_{k}^{(t,i)}-\gamma\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}_{k}^{(t,i)},\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(t,i)}),\ i=0,\ldots,\tau-1,

    where γ\gamma is the learning rate, and 𝒟k(t,i)\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(t,i)} is a randomly sampled mini-batch of data from 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k}.

  3. 3.

    Each client computes its local model update 𝒈k(t)=𝒙k(t,τ)−𝒙(t){\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}={\bm{x}}_{k}^{(t,\tau)}-{\bm{x}}^{(t)} and sends it to the PS.11 1 With single-step SGD, i.e., τ=1\tau=1, the local model update equals the negative of the local gradient multiplied by the step size.

  4. 4.

    The PSaggregates all updates to obtain the new global model:

    𝒙(t+1)=𝒙(t)+∑k=1Kwk​𝒈k(t).\displaystyle{\bm{x}}^{(t+1)}={\bm{x}}^{(t)}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}. (2)

Many variations of FedAvghave been proposed, such as reducing variance by computing and communicating auxiliary correction vectors [20, 55], introducing momentum in local updates [31], or adding a proximal term to improve stability in heterogeneous settings [28].

Communication Bottleneck

In each round of the distributed training procedure, FedAvgrequires two communication phases: (1) clients upload local updates to the PS; and (2) the PSbroadcasts the updated global model. Most existing research on communication-efficient FLfocuses on client-to-PSlinks, since each client requires dedicated resources to transmit its model update to the PS. To reduce the communication cost, data compression is commonly applied before transmitting the local model updates. Let {𝒈^k(t)}k=1,…,K\{\widehat{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}\}_{k=1,\ldots,K} represent the reconstructed local model updates at the PS, a common design principle for compression is to minimize the distortion measured by the empirical mean square error (MSE), given by

MSE​(𝒈^k(t),𝒈k(t))=1d​∥𝒈^k(t)−𝒈k(t)∥2.\textnormal{MSE}(\widehat{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)})=\frac{1}{d}\lVert\widehat{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}-{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}\rVert^{2}. (3)

Many existing works use this distortion measure implicitly or explicitly, as we will discuss later.

Earlier studies on FLwith compressed updates focus on simple schemes such as sparsification or masking. Recent studies have adopted different forms of subspace projection methods, motivated by the potential correlation/redundancy in transmitted information [46, 2, 50, 51, 1, 6]. Nevertheless, current literature lacks a unified taxonomy to describe and interpret how specific compression designs relate to different sources of correlation inherent in FLalgorithms. We categorize them into three types:

  • •

    Structural correlation results from the learning model, e.g., neural network structure. Some components of the gradient vectors may be correlated with other components.

  • •

    Temporal correlation originates from the iterative nature of the optimization algorithm and is influenced by design features such as momentum and regularization. As a result, gradient vectors generated in consecutive iterations may exhibit significant correlation.

  • •

    Spatial correlation arises when training datasets across different clients share similar distributions. This can lead to correlated local model updates across clients.

In the following sections, we discuss each correlation type in detail and provide illustrative examples. While a complete theoretical understanding of these correlations remains elusive – partly due to the black-box nature of deep learning models [53] – we aim to offer practical insight and useful tools for analyzing and exploiting them.

III Structural Correlation

We define structural correlation as the dependency among the elements within a client’s local model update 𝒈k(t){\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}. Let us consider a simple linear regression example. Given a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} containg NN pairs of feature-observation points (𝝃i,yi)∈ℝd−1×ℝ({\bm{\xi}}_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}, i∈[N]i\in[N], we form a prediction function y^i\widehat{y}_{i} using a linear model

yi^​(𝒘,b)=𝝃i𝖳​𝒘+b,\displaystyle\widehat{y_{i}}({\bm{w}},b)={\bm{\xi}}_{i}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{w}}+b, (4)

where 𝒘∈ℝd−1{\bm{w}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1} is the weight vector and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} is the bias. The objective is to find the estimate of 𝒘{\bm{w}} and bb such that the corresponding elements of 𝒚^=(y^1,…,y^N)𝖳∈ℝN\widehat{{\bm{y}}}=(\widehat{y}_{1},\dots,\widehat{y}_{N})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and 𝒚=(y1,…,yN)𝖳∈ℝN{\bm{y}}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{N})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} are as close as possible for all samples i∈𝒟i\in\mathcal{D}. Using vector notation, we obtain 𝒚^​(𝒙)=R​𝒙\widehat{{\bm{y}}}({\bm{x}})=R{\bm{x}}, where R=[𝝃1,…,𝝃N;𝟏N𝖳]𝖳∈ℝN×dR=[{\bm{\xi}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{\xi}}_{N};\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}]^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, and 𝒙=[𝒘;b]∈ℝd{\bm{x}}=[{\bm{w}};b]\in\mathbb{R}^{d} collects all tunable parameters.

We quantify the quality of the fit using the MSEover all NN samples. The objective and its gradient are

f⁡(𝒙)=∥𝒚^​(𝒙)−𝒚∥2N=𝒙𝖳​R𝖳​R​𝒙−2​𝒚𝖳​R​𝒙+𝒚𝖳​𝒚N\displaystyle f({\bm{x}})=\frac{\lVert\widehat{{\bm{y}}}({\bm{x}})-{\bm{y}}\rVert^{2}}{N}=\frac{{\bm{x}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R{\bm{x}}-2{\bm{y}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R{\bm{x}}+{\bm{y}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}}{N} (5)

and

∇f​(𝒙)=1N​(2​R𝖳​R​𝒙−2​R𝖳​𝒚),\displaystyle\nabla f({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{N}\left(2R^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R{\bm{x}}-2R^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}\right), (6)

respectively. These expressions display how the dataset RR and the objective function f⁡(𝒙)f({\bm{x}}) interact to potentially induce correlations among the components of ∇f​(𝒙)\nabla f({\bm{x}}).

For more complex tasks with larger MLmodels, several existing works have investigated the existence of such structural correlation. For instance, [15] and [11] show that the gradient converges to a very small subspace spanned by a few top eigenvectors of the Hessian. This suggests that dimension reduction can be achieved by projecting the gradients onto a low-dimensional subspace [27]. The impact of the network model and data on the spectrum of the Hessian matrix has been investigated in [40]. The observations can also be related to the intrinsic dimensionality of data and model representations [5, 26], suggesting that high-dimensional models with a large number of parameters may effectively be trained within a lower-dimensional subspace.

III-A How to Evaluate the Degree of Structural Correlation?

First, consider the local model update vector 𝒈k(t)∈ℝd{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we introduce the model update matrix generated by client kk at iteration tt as

Gk(t)=(𝒈k,1(t)…𝒈k,n(t))∈ℝm×n,\displaystyle G_{k}^{(t)}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{g}}_{k,1}^{(t)}&\dots&{\bm{g}}_{k,n}^{(t)}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, (7)

where 𝒈k,i(t)∈ℝm{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the ii-column of Gk(t)G_{k}^{(t)}. This matrix contains the elements of 𝒈k(t)∈ℝd{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, reshaped into an m×nm\times n matrix such that m​n=dmn=d.22 2 If dd is not divisible by mm, zero-padding will be applied. We refer to each column 𝒈k,i(t){\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)} as a model update slice. The structural correlation may depend on the organization of the model update matrix, as evidenced in [51, 45, 47], where different choices for the mapping from vector 𝒈k(t){\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)} to matrix Gk(t)G_{k}^{(t)} have been considered.

The cosine similarity is used to measure the degree of structural correlation between two model update slices:

CSS⁡(𝒈k,i(t),𝒈k,j(t))={(𝒈k,i(t))𝖳​𝒈k,j(t)∥𝒈k,i(t)∥​∥𝒈k,j(t)∥,𝒈k,i(t)≠𝟎​and​𝒈k,j(t)≠𝟎0,otherwise\css({\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}_{k,j}^{(t)})\!=\!\begin{cases}\frac{({\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{g}}_{k,j}^{(t)}}{\lVert{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}\rVert\lVert{\bm{g}}_{k,j}^{(t)}\rVert},&{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}\!\neq\!\mathbf{0}\penalty\ \text{and}\penalty\ {\bm{g}}_{k,j}^{(t)}\!\neq\!\mathbf{0}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

where ii and jj are slice indices. In FL, if different model update slices of the model update matrix exhibit high pairwise cosine similarity, it becomes possible to identify a common subspace to represent these model update slices effectively. This enables a more efficient, lower-dimensional representation, which is the main motivation behind many compression designs using low-rank approximation.

Another way to quantify the degree of structural correlation is to use singular value decomposition (SVD). A matrix G∈ℝm×nG\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} can be decomposed as

G=U​Σ​V𝖳,\displaystyle G=U\Sigma V^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}, (8)

where U∈ℝm×mU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and V∈ℝn×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} are orthonormal matrices, and Σ∈ℝm×n\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} contains the singular values σ1,…,σmin⁡{m,n}\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{\min\{m,n\}} on its main diagonal, in decreasing order σ1≥⋯≥σmin⁡{m,n}≥0\sigma_{1}\geq\dots\geq\sigma_{\min\{m,n\}}\geq 0. SVDenables the identification of global correlations among multiple vectors, rather than local pairwise correlations, albeit at a higher computational cost than the cosine similarity metric. When applying SVDto the model update matrix, the presence of a few dominant singular values suggests a stronger low-rank structure.

III-B Exploiting Structural Correlation using Low-Rank Approximation

Once a high degree of structural correlation is observed within each local model update, low-rank approximation can be applied to obtain a compressed update of reduced dimension.

SVD

One example of low-rank approximation is to perform SVDon the model update matrix Gk(t)=U​Σ​V𝖳G_{k}^{(t)}=U\Sigma V^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}, where U∈ℝm×mU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and V∈ℝn×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} are orthogonal matrices and Σ\Sigma contains the singular values. A lower-dimensional representation of Gk(t)G_{k}^{(t)} can be formed using Ur∈ℝm×rU_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} and Vr∈ℝn×rV_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, whose columns are the first rr columns of UU and VV respectively, i.e., Ur=[U]:,1:rU_{r}=[U]_{:,1:r} and Vr=[V]:,1:rV_{r}=[V]_{:,1:r}. Model update compression can use either UrU_{r} alone or the combination of UrU_{r} and VrV_{r}.

  • •

    When compression uses only UrU_{r}, client kk transmits the compressed update Ur𝖳​Gk(t)∈ℝr×nU_{r}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}G_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} to the PS. An example of using SVDto compress local model updates is the ATOMO framework presented in [47].

Remark III.1.

By ranking the singular values in decreasing order, and sending the basis vectors corresponding to the rr largest singular values, the compression design effectively minimizes the MSEdistortion of the reconstructed model update, under a limited number of transmitted elements.

PCA

This is achieved by computing a covariance matrix CC from the columns of Gk(t)G_{k}^{(t)} and performing the eigenvalue decomposition C=Q​Λ​Q𝖳C=Q\Lambda Q^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}, where Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λm)\Lambda=\diag(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}) is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, with λ1≥⋯≥λm≥0\lambda_{1}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{m}\geq 0, and Q∈ℝm×mQ\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is an orthonormal matrix. C=1n−1​∑i′=1n(𝒈k,i′(t)−𝒈¯)​(𝒈k,i′(t)−𝒈¯)𝖳.C=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{n}({\bm{g}}_{k,i^{\prime}}^{(t)}-\bar{{\bm{g}}})({\bm{g}}_{k,i^{\prime}}^{(t)}-\bar{{\bm{g}}})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}. (9)

which is then transmitted to the PS. After the PSreceives the compressed model update slice from client kk, it can get an estimate of the model update slice by

𝒈^k,i(t)=Qr​𝒈~(t)+𝒈¯=Qr​Qr𝖳​(𝒈k,i(t)−𝒈¯)+𝒈¯∈ℝm.\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{g}}}_{k,i}^{(t)}=Q_{r}\widetilde{{\bm{g}}}^{(t)}+\bar{{\bm{g}}}=Q_{r}Q_{r}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}({\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}-\bar{{\bm{g}}})+\bar{{\bm{g}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. (11)

Remark III.2.

The PCAand SVDare closely related [13]. For example, when 𝐠¯=𝟎m\bar{{\bm{g}}}=\mathbf{0}_{m}, the squared singular values σi2\sigma^{2}_{i} coincide with the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix λi\lambda_{i}, and the left unitary matrix UU coincides with the PCAbasis QQ.

For both PCAand SVD, it is obvious that the choice of rr (the number of basis vectors to be communicated) plays a critical role. Larger values of rr capture more information in the subspace spanned by the model update matrix, while smaller values of rr reduce the communication cost. There is always a trade-off among information loss, computational complexity, and communication cost.

IV Temporal Correlation

In the context of FL, temporal correlation refers to the similarity between consecutive local model updates 𝒈k(t),𝒈k(t+1),…{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t+1)},\ldots, generated by each client kk. In general, the degree of temporal correlation may be affected by the following factors:

  • •

    Properties of the loss function, e.g., convexity, and smoothness. With a convex and smooth global objective function, we expect stronger temporal correlation compared to a non-convex function with many local minima.

  • •

    Hyperparameter values in the iterative optimization algorithm, e.g., learning rate, batch size, momentum, and regularization factor.

Figure 1 shows the trajectory of the parameter vector (with two parameters) in a linear regression problem. We observe that a smaller learning rate yields a smoother trajectory, implying a higher degree of temporal correlation, albeit at the cost of requiring more iterations to converge.

IV-A How to Evaluate the Degree of Temporal Correlation?

The degree of temporal correlation can be quantified using the cosine similarity between two model update vectors, i.e., CSS⁡(𝒈k(t1),𝒈k(t2))\css({\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t_{1})},{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t_{2})}), where t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} are two time (iteration) indices. A high degree of similarity suggests that past model updates can be leveraged to predict the trajectory of future updates, which is the main motivation behind prediction-based model update compression schemes.

For the linear regression problem with a quadratic loss function, we can obtain a closed-form expression for the degree of temporal correlation. Combining the gradient vector in (6) with the parameter update 𝒙(t+1)=𝒙(t)−γ∇f(𝒙(t)){\bm{x}}^{(t+1)}={\bm{x}}^{(t)}-\gamma\nabla f({\bm{x}}^{(t)}), we get

=\displaystyle= ∇f(𝒙(t))−γ2​R𝖳​RN∇f(𝒙(t))\displaystyle\nabla f({\bm{x}}^{(t)})-\gamma\frac{2R^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R}{N}\nabla f({\bm{x}}^{(t)})

where λi​(A)\lambda_{i}(A) is the ii-th eigenvalue of AA. Naturally, this means that a smaller learning rate and a smaller LL lead to a higher degree of temporal correlation.

IV-B Exploiting Temporal Correlation using Predictive Coding

Predictive coding techniques are widely used in multimedia compression scenarios to reduce redundancy by exploiting correlations between adjacent pixels or image frames [42, 41]. In FL, prediction-based encoding has been used to exploit the temporal correlation between consecutive model updates [52, 34, 37, 2, 9, 12]. The key idea is to generate a prediction 𝒈widecheckk(t)\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)} of the current model update based on the knowledge of previous updates {𝒈k(t−1),𝒈k(t−2),…}\{{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t-1)},{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t-2)},\ldots\} and transmit only the prediction residual 𝒈k(t)−𝒈widecheckk(t){\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}-\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}, i.e., the difference between the actual update and the prediction. The PScomputes the same prediction using shared information between the clients, based on which it can reconstruct the original model update after receiving the residual. When the prediction is accurate, the residual contains much less information than the original model update, and can therefore be represented using fewer bits. Communication efficiency can be further improved by omitting residual transmission when the prediction is sufficiently accurate [12, 6]. The predictor can, e.g.,

  • •

    the previous local model update (e.g., gradient vector when using single-step SGD) [34, 37], so that the prediction residual becomes the model update difference;

  • •

    momentum-inspired weighted average of previous local model updates [2, 9];

  • •

    linear combination of previous model updates with combination weights optimized by the least-squares criterion (i.e., minimizing the MSE distortion) [12, 6].

Particularly, in [12], the prediction relies on a window of previously transmitted model updates {𝒈^(t−t′)}t′=1,…,h\{\widehat{{\bm{g}}}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{t^{\prime}=1,\dots,h}, which are combined through a linear predictor defined as

𝒈widechecklin(t)​(𝒂)=∑t′=1hat′​𝒈^(t−t′).\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{\textrm{lin}}^{(t)}({\bm{a}})=\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{h}a_{t^{\prime}}\widehat{{\bm{g}}}^{(t-t^{\prime})}. (14)

Here, 𝒂=[a1,…,ah]{\bm{a}}=[a_{1},\ldots,a_{h}] contains the prediction coefficients and hh is the memory size. The optimal coefficients 𝒂∗(t)∈ℝh{\bm{a}}^{*}{}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{h} are found by minimizing the reconstruction error between the current model update 𝒈(t){\bm{g}}^{(t)} and the prediction 𝒈widechecklin(t)​(𝒂)\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{\textrm{lin}}^{(t)}({\bm{a}}), i.e.,

𝒂∗=(t)arg⁡min𝐚∈ℝh∥𝐠widechecklin(t)(𝐚)−𝐠(t)∥2.{\bm{a}}^{*}{}^{(t)}=\argmin_{{\bm{a}}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}}\lVert\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{\textrm{lin}}^{(t)}({\bm{a}})-{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\rVert^{2}. (15)

The predictor can also be written in a matrix form 𝒈widecheckk,lin(t)​(𝒂)=M​𝒂\widecheck{{\bm{g}}}_{k,\text{lin}}^{(t)}({\bm{a}})=M{\bm{a}}, where M=(𝒈k(t−1),…,𝒈k(t−h))∈ℝd×hM=({\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t-1)},\dots,{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t-h)})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times h}. When MM has full column rank, the MSE-optimal prediction coefficients can be obtained in closed-form as 𝒂∗=(t)(M𝖳M)−1M𝖳𝒈(t){\bm{a}}^{*}{}^{(t)}=(M^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}M)^{-1}M^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{g}}^{(t)}. This corresponds to projecting 𝒈(t){\bm{g}}^{(t)} onto the subspace spanned by the columns of MM.

V Spatial Correlation

We define spatial correlation as the similarity between local model updates 𝒈k(t){\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)} produced by different clients k∈[K]k\in[K]. A primary source of spatial correlation is the training data available to each client. When clients’ local datasets are drawn from similar distributions, spatial correlation tends to be high. In FL, local datasets are very often statistically heterogeneous and unbalanced, which affects the degree of spatial correlation that can be observed during the training procedure [29, 30].

V-A How to Evaluate the Degree of Spatial Correlation?

The degree of spatial correlation between two clients can be quantified by the cosine similarity of their local model updates, i.e., CSS⁡(𝒈k(t),𝒈l(t))\css({\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}_{l}^{(t)}), where kk and ll are two client indices. When the model update vectors from multiple clients are highly correlated, it is possible to identify a common lower-dimensional subspace that efficiently represents these updates. Note that exploiting spatial correlation locally is difficult for individual clients unless each one has precise knowledge of the common subspace. Therefore, it requires the assistance of the PS, which has knowledge of all local model updates.

Again, we use the linear regression example to illustrate the effects of spatial correlation. We consider two clients kk and ll, each with NkN_{k} and NlN_{l} data samples. The local loss functions are given by fk​(𝒙)=1Nk​(𝒙𝖳​Rk𝖳​Rk​𝒙−2​𝒚k𝖳​Rk​𝒙+𝒚k𝖳​𝒚k)f_{k}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{N_{k}}({\bm{x}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}{\bm{x}}-2{\bm{y}}_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}{\bm{x}}+{\bm{y}}_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{k}), and fl​(𝒙)=1Nl​(𝒙𝖳​Rl𝖳​Rl​𝒙−2​𝒚l𝖳​Rl​𝒙+𝒚l𝖳​𝒚l)f_{l}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{N_{l}}({\bm{x}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}{\bm{x}}-2{\bm{y}}_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}{\bm{x}}+{\bm{y}}_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{l}), respectively. The cosine similarity between their gradient vectors is

CSS⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle\css( OPEN∇fk​(𝒙),∇fl​(𝒙))\displaystyle\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}),\nabla f_{l}({\bm{x}}))
=\displaystyle= (Rk𝖳​Rk​𝒙−Rk𝖳​𝒚k)𝖳​(Rl𝖳​Rl​𝒙−Rl𝖳​𝒚l)Nk​Nl​∥∇fk​(𝒙(t))∥​∥∇fl​(𝒙(t))∥\displaystyle\frac{(R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}{\bm{x}}-R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{k})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}(R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}{\bm{x}}-R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{l})}{N_{k}N_{l}\lVert\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}^{(t)})\rVert\lVert\nabla f_{l}({\bm{x}}^{(t)})\rVert}

where A=Rk𝖳​RkNk​Rl𝖳​RlNlA=\frac{R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}}{N_{k}}\frac{R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}}{N_{l}}, 𝒃𝖳=−1Nk​Nl​(𝒚k𝖳​Rk​Rl𝖳​Rl+𝒚l𝖳​Rl​Rk𝖳​Rk){\bm{b}}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}=\frac{-1}{N_{k}N_{l}}({\bm{y}}_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}+{\bm{y}}_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}), and c=1Nk​Nl​(𝒚k𝖳​Rk​Rl𝖳​𝒚l)c=\frac{1}{N_{k}N_{l}}({\bm{y}}_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{l}). The gradient of the quadratic loss is invariant under unitary transformations of the column space. Specifically, if Rl=P​RkR_{l}=PR_{k} and 𝒚l=P​𝒚k{\bm{y}}_{l}=P{\bm{y}}_{k}, for any orthonormal P∈ℝNk×NkP\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{k}\times N_{k}}, then ∇fl​(𝒙)=Rl𝖳​Rl​𝒙−Rl𝖳​𝒚l=Rk𝖳​P𝖳​P​Rk​𝒙−Rk𝖳​P𝖳​P​𝒚k=Rk𝖳​Rk​𝒙−Rk𝖳​𝒚k=∇fk​(𝒙)\nabla f_{l}({\bm{x}})=R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{l}{\bm{x}}-R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{l}=R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}P^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}PR_{k}{\bm{x}}-R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}P^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}P{\bm{y}}_{k}=R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}R_{k}{\bm{x}}-R_{k}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{y}}_{k}=\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}). Since the cosine similarity between any vector and itself is one, it follows that CSS⁡(∇fk​(𝒙),∇fl​(𝒙))=1\css(\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}),\nabla f_{l}({\bm{x}}))=1 in this case.

By examining the row space further, we can identify two cases where CSS⁡(∇fk​(𝒙),∇fl​(𝒙))=0\css(\nabla f_{k}({\bm{x}}),\nabla f_{l}({\bm{x}}))=0. First, if the row spaces of RlR_{l} and RkR_{k} are orthogonal, i.e., Rk​Rl𝖳=𝟎Nk×NlR_{k}R_{l}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{0}_{N_{k}\times N_{l}}, the cosine similarity is zero, which corresponds to the scenario of extreme data heterogeneity. Otherwise, we obtain a level hypersurface of the quadratic function at which the cosine similarity is zero. Note that this set of points includes the minimizers of fk​(𝒙)f_{k}({\bm{x}}) and fl​(𝒙)f_{l}({\bm{x}}). In the remaining parameter space, the cosine similarity is nonzero, indicating the existence of potential correlations that could be exploited for compression.

Quantifying spatial correlation between more than two clients is possible using a SVD-based measure. To facilitate this, we generalize the method in Section III-B by considering the observation matrix Φ∈ℝp×q\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}. The structure of Φ\Phi depends on the type of correlation we aim to measure. To measure spatial correlation in FL, we use Φ=(𝒈1(t),…,𝒈K(t))∈ℝd×K\Phi=({\bm{g}}_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,{\bm{g}}_{K}^{(t)})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K}, which contains the local gradient vectors from all clients, available at the PS. To measure structural correlation, we take Φ=Gk(t)∈ℝm×n\Phi=G_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, as in Section III-B.

Applying SVDto the measurement matrix gives Φ=U​Σ​V𝖳\Phi=U\Sigma V^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}, where Σ∈ℝp×q\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q} contains the singular values σi,i∈[min⁡{p,q}]\sigma_{i},\ i\in[\min\{p,q\}], sorted as σ1≥..≥σmin⁡{p,q}\sigma_{1}\geq..\geq\sigma_{\min\{p,q\}}, on its diagonal elements, and U∈ℝp×pU\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} and V∈ℝq×qV\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q} are orthonormal matrices.

Definition V.1 (Conserved Energy Ratio).

Given an observation matrix Φ∈ℝp×q\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}, and r∈[0,min⁡{p,q}]r\in[0,\min\{p,q\}], the energy conserved by the first rr singular values is defined as

αcer=∑i=1rσi2/∑i=1min⁡{p,q}σi2=∥Σ1:r,1:r∥F2/∥Σ∥F2.\displaystyle\alpha_{\mathrm{cer}}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}^{2}\Big/\mspace{-5mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\min\{p,q\}}\sigma_{i}^{2}=\lVert\Sigma_{\rm 1:r,1:r}\rVert_{F}^{2}/\lVert\Sigma\rVert_{F}^{2}. (17)

Using Definition V.1, we define a measurement function MCorrSVD(Φ,βsvd)\textnormal{MCorrSVD}\mathopen{}(\Phi,\beta_{\text{\rm svd}}), where the inputs are:

  • •

    an observation matrix Φ∈ℝp×q\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}, and

  • •

    a fraction βsvd∈[0,1]\beta_{\text{\rm svd}}\in[0,1],

and the output is the conserved energy ratio αcer∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{cer}}\in[0,1] for r=⌈βsvd⋅min⁡{p,q}⌉r=\lceil\beta_{\text{\rm svd}}\cdot\min\{p,q\}\rceil. This function quantifies the proportion of energy captured by a low-rank approximation using a fraction βsvd\beta_{\text{svd}} of the leading singular values. As an example, for some energy threshold αsvd∈[0,1]\alpha_{\text{svd}}\in[0,1], we can consider sufficient correlation to be present if MCorrSVD(Φ,βsvd)=αcer≥αsvd\textnormal{MCorrSVD}\mathopen{}(\Phi,\beta_{\text{svd}})=\alpha_{\mathrm{cer}}\geq\alpha_{\textrm{svd}}.

While this heuristic rule can be applied, other metrics such as the effective rank [39] could provide a more principled way to quantify the extent of low-rank structure.

V-B Exploiting Spatial Correlation using Subspace Projection

In addition to measuring the correlation degree, SVDcan also be used to extract a subspace onto which we project the model update, thereby reducing its dimensionality. After collecting local model updates from all clients, the PSperforms SVDon the measurement matrix Φ=(𝒈1(t),…,𝒈K(t))∈ℝd×K\Phi=({\bm{g}}_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,{\bm{g}}_{K}^{(t)})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} as Φ=U​Σ​V𝖳\Phi=U\Sigma V^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}. Then, we define an operator TruncSVD(Φ,αsvd)\textnormal{TruncSVD}\mathopen{}(\Phi,\alpha_{\text{svd}}), which, given inputs

  • •

    an observation matrix Φ∈ℝp×q\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}, and

  • •

    a threshold αsvd∈[0,1]\alpha_{\text{svd}}\in[0,1],

returns the truncated SVD components

  • •

    Σr=Σ1:r,1:r∈ℝr×r\Sigma_{r}=\Sigma_{1:r,1:r}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},

  • •

    Ur=U:,1:r∈ℝp×rU_{r}=U_{:,1:r}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}, and

  • •

    Vr=V:,1:r∈ℝq×rV_{r}=V_{:,1:r}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r},

where rr is selected as the smallest integer such that the conserved energy ratio (see Definition V.1) is above the target value αsvd\alpha_{\text{\rm svd}}. The PSneeds to broadcast UrU_{r} (and possibly VrV_{r}) to all clients so that they can perform model update compression by subspace projection in subsequent iterations. For example, when using Ur∈ℝd×rU_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} to compress the model update vector 𝒈k(t)∈ℝd{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have the compressed model update as

𝒈~k(t)=Ur𝖳​𝒈k(t),\displaystyle\widetilde{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}=U_{r}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}, (18)

which reduces the number of transmitted elements from dd to rr. After the PSreceives 𝒈~k(t)\widetilde{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}, it can recover an approximate model update by

𝒈^k(t)=Ur​𝒈~k(t)=Ur​Ur𝖳​𝒈k(t).\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}=U_{r}\widetilde{{\bm{g}}}_{k}^{(t)}=U_{r}U_{r}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}. (19)
Remark V.1.

The SVD-based low-rank approximation method presented in Section III-B projects the current model update matrix GG onto its top-rr singular subspace. The subspace projection method presented in this section uses a fixed subspace with previously learned basis from an earlier iteration. The difference is that exploiting spatial correlation among clients requires server-side processing, i.e., the PScollects local updates to extract subspace information for client-side compression in later iterations.

VI Benefits and Limitations of Subspace Projection Methods

While the idea of using subspace projection for model update compression in FLis not new, our correlation-based taxonomy provides a unified lens for understanding the underlying design principles. In this section, we will classify existing studies into different categories, and discuss the benefits and limitations of these methods in terms of communication cost, computational, and memory overhead.

VI-A Classification of Existing Compression Methods

Table I gathers and classifies some existing correlation-aware compression methods, depending on the sources of correlation they rely on. Next, we discuss some of them in more detail.

VI-A1 Temporal Sparsification Mask

The works in [35, 44] consider sparsification in the standard parameter basis and are therefore classified as exploiting structural correlation. These schemes leverage temporal correlation by retaining part of the sparsification mask across consecutive iterations, implicitly assuming temporal correlation. Moreover, [44] is also classified as exploiting spatial correlation because the portion of the mask preserved between iterations is shared across all clients.

VI-A2 GradiVeQ

The work in [51] adopts an alternative transmission protocol, known as ring-all-reduce, which provides all clients with access to the aggregated model update once communication is complete. The update is divided into model update slices, similarly to the approach used in this paper. The method alternates between two phases: a training phase and a compression phase. During the training phase, each client stores model updates, after which a covariance matrix is computed. Temporal correlation is exploited by using PCA, and the basis matrix learned from the first slice is reused for all subsequent slices. We classify this use of structural and temporal correlations as implicit, since a single basis matrix is reused across slices and across multiple iterations.

VI-A3 SVDFed

The work in [46] employs server-assisted compression to capture spatial correlation among clients using SVD. It uses Φ=(𝒈1(t),…,𝒈K(t))\Phi=({\bm{g}}_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,{\bm{g}}_{K}^{(t)}), and performs compression using a truncated left orthonormal matrix UrU_{r}.

These prior studies typically assume that the sources of correlation they rely on always exist. In practice, algorithm designers should verify the strength of these correlations and adapt the compression scheme accordingly, rather than applying one-size-fits-all compressors.

VI-B Communication Cost Reduction

The main advantage of subspace projection as a compression method is the reduced communication cost. Instead of transmitting dd (entire parameter vector) or mm (one slice of the model update matrix) elements, only rr elements need to be transmitted. However, the basis matrix is needed for both the clients and the PSto perform compression and decompression. Transmitting the basis matrix incurs additional communication cost, and the amount of extra communicated information depends on whether the clients or PScompute the basis matrices. When using client-side processing, the basis matrices are computed at each client and communicated to the PS, thus the communication cost grows linearly with the number of clients KK. When using server-side processing, the basis matrices are computed at the PSand sent back to the clients, which can be done by broadcast.

The break-even point in terms of the total number of communicated elements can be easily calculated for each compression method. Consider an example where we use server-side processing and want to compress one model update slice of the model update matrix, 𝒈k,i(t){\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}, using TruncSVD((𝒈1,i(t),…,𝒈K,i(t)),α)\textnormal{TruncSVD}\mathopen{}(({\bm{g}}_{1,i}^{(t)},\ldots,{\bm{g}}_{K,i}^{(t)}),\alpha), for some α\alpha. If we reuse UrU_{r} for jj consecutive iterations, the total communication cost is m​r+r​jmr+rj, for transmitting UrU_{r} and Ur𝖳​𝒈k,i(t)U_{r}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)}. Uncompressed model updates for the same number of iterations require transmitting j​mjm elements. When m​r+r​j<j​m⇔j>m​rm−rmr+rj<jm\iff j>\frac{mr}{m-r}, reusing the basis vectors over multiple iterations reduces the total communication cost. Nevertheless, this calculation ignores that compression will introduce distortion into the model updates, potentially affecting training performance.

For example, suppose consecutive gradient iterates maintain a cosine similarity of at least cc, so the angle between them is at most θ=arccos⁡(c)\theta=\arccos(c). After jj iterations, the angle between 𝒈(t){\bm{g}}^{(t)} and 𝒈(t−j){\bm{g}}^{(t-j)} can be as large as j​θj\theta, giving CSS(𝒈(t),𝒈(t−j))≥cos(jθ)\css({\bm{g}}^{(t)},\mathopen{}{\bm{g}}^{(t-j)})\geq\cos(j\theta). To guarantee temporal correlation, we require j≤2​πθj\leq\frac{2\pi}{\theta}. If the break-even number of iterations m​rm−r\frac{mr}{m-r} exceeds this limit, reusing the basis matrix for that many iterations is not guaranteed to be useful.

VI-C Implicit Dependence on Temporal Correlation

A limitation of server-side computation of basis matrices is that after the PScollects local model updates from all clients in iteration tt, the extracted basis matrices can only be used for update compression in the subsequent iterations t+1,t+2,…t+1,t+2,\ldots. Consequently, such compression methods rely on the implicit assumption of temporal correlation, meaning that the subspace information extracted from earlier iterations can remain useful later. With weak temporal correlation, the basis matrix will fail to capture the model evolution in subsequent iterations, thus resulting in high compression distortion.

VI-D Computational and Memory Overhead

Using SVDor PCAfor measuring correlation and designing compression schemes requires additional computations. For example, if we want to verify the degree of structural correlation before applying low-rank approximation to compress a model update matrix Gk(t)∈ℝm×nG_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, we only need to compute its singular values, and not the full SVD. If m≥nm\geq n, computating singular values requiring 𝒪(2mn2+2n3)\mathcal{O}\mathopen{}(2mn^{2}+2n^{3}) FLOPS, compared to 𝒪(6mn2+20n3)\mathcal{O}\mathopen{}(6mn^{2}+20n^{3}) FLOPS for the complete SVD[14, Section 8.6]. Computing PCA, especially for tall matrices with m≫nm\gg n, by explicitly forming the covariance matrix may be inefficient. Instead, one can exploit the close relationship between PCAand SVDto obtain the principal components and singular values of the covariance matrix directly via an SVD [13]. Moreover, since PCArequires mean subtraction—incurring an additional cost of m⁡(n+1)m(n+1) FLOPS—it typically entails higher computational overhead than SVD.

Memory overhead originates from the need to store previous model update information, such as in temporal-correlation-aware compression design via predictive coding, which consumes storage resources. When the number of clients grows, this memory overhead may become a significant concern.

VII Adaptive Compression Designs with Multiple Sources of Correlation

The three types of correlation may coexist in an FLsystem. Thus, an efficient compression design can benefit from jointly considering multiple sources of correlation. In this section, we introduce two adaptive and context-aware compression designs: AdaSVDFed in Section VII-A, an augmented version of SVDFed, and PCAFed in Section VII-B, which can exploit all three types of correlation when present and switch between different compression modes depending on the degree of measured correlation.

VII-A AdaSVDFed

We introduce AdaSVDFed in Algorithm 1, which switches between SVD-based and predictive-coding-based compression modes depending on the measured spatial correlation. Every TuT_{u} iterations, the algorithm enters an update state s=UPDATEs=\textnormal{UPDATE}, where the PSmeasures spatial correlation to decide whether SVDFed compression in [46] or predictive-coding compression in [12] will be used for the next Tu−1T_{u}-1 iterations. Specifically, the switching decision is governed by βSF∈[0,1]\beta_{\mathrm{SF}}\in[0,1] and αSF∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{SF}}\in[0,1]: we set s=SPATIALs=\textnormal{SPATIAL} and use SVDFed compression (described in Section VI-A3) if no more than ⌈βSF⋅min⁡{K,d}⌉\lceil\beta_{\mathrm{SF}}\cdot\min\{K,d\}\rceil basis vectors are needed to capture at least a fraction αSF\alpha_{\mathrm{SF}} of the energy in (𝒈1(t),…,𝒈K(t))({\bm{g}}_{1}^{(t)},\dots,{\bm{g}}_{K}^{(t)}). Otherwise, we set s=PREDs=\textnormal{PRED} to use the predictive-coding mode (described in Section IV-B), in which each client further compresses the prediction residual using 𝒞(⋅):ℝd→ℝp\mathcal{C}\mathopen{}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{p} (e.g., sparsification) and the PSreconstructs the vector via the reverse operation EXPAND​(⋅):ℝp→ℝd\textnormal{EXPAND}(\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}. The key advantage of AdaSVDFed is that it avoids transmitting the basis matrix UrU_{r} from the PSto the clients when the spatial correlation is low, thereby reducing downlink communication cost when the basis provides little compression benefit.

Note that both SVD and predictive coding methods already exist in the literature. With this AdaSVDFed algorithm, our goal is to demonstrate that introducing an adaptive switching mechanism can improve existing compression designs, as shown in Section VIII through simulation results.

VII-B PCAFed

Until now, SVDhas been the primary method considered for measuring and exploiting correlations. An alternative option is to use PCA, as discussed in Sections III-A and III-B. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a set of pp-dimensional vectors, for instance, 𝒢={𝒈k,i(t−t′)}i∈[n],t′∈[h]\mathcal{G}=\{{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{i\in[n],t^{\prime}\in[h]} with p=mp=m, which contains all model update slices (with lenght mm) of client kk in multiple iterations. In this way, we can jointly measure the temporal and structural correlations. Compute the mean 𝝁=1/|𝒢|∑𝒈′∈𝒢𝒈′∈ℝp{\bm{\mu}}=1/|\mathcal{G}|\sum_{{\bm{g}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}}{\bm{g}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and the covariance

C=1|𝒢|−1​∑𝒈′∈𝒢(𝒈′−𝝁)​(𝒈′−𝝁)𝖳∈ℝp×p.C=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|-1}\sum_{{\bm{g}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}}({\bm{g}}^{\prime}-{\bm{\mu}})({\bm{g}}^{\prime}-{\bm{\mu}})^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}. (20)

We find the principal values λi,i=1,…,p\lambda_{i},\penalty\ i=1,\dots,p, from the eigenvalue decomposition C=Q​Λ​Q𝖳C=Q\Lambda Q^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}, where Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λp)\Lambda=\diag(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{p}) is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, ordered such that λ1≥⋯≥λp≥0\lambda_{1}\geq\dots\geq\lambda_{p}\geq 0, and Q∈ℝp×pQ\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} is an orthonormal matrix. To measure the degree of correlation using PCA, we consider the approximate energy ratio defined as

αaer=∥𝝁∥22+∑i=1rλi∥𝝁∥22+∑i=1pλi.\displaystyle\alpha_{\mathrm{aer}}=\frac{\lVert{\bm{\mu}}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_{i}}{\lVert{\bm{\mu}}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\lambda_{i}}. (21)

Then, using (21), we define a measurement function MCorrPCA(𝒢,βpca)\textnormal{MCorrPCA}\mathopen{}(\mathcal{G},\beta_{\textrm{pca}}), where the inputs are:

  • •

    a set of pp-dimensional vectors 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and

  • •

    a fraction βpca∈[0,1]\beta_{\textrm{pca}}\in[0,1],

and the output is the approximate energy ratio αaer∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{aer}}\in[0,1] for r=⌈βpca⋅p⌉r=\lceil\beta_{\textrm{pca}}\cdot p\rceil. This function provides an approximate method for quantifying the energy captured by a low-rank subspace. As an example, for a threshold αpca∈[0,1]\alpha_{\textrm{pca}}\in[0,1], we consider correlation to be sufficient if MCorrPCA(𝒢,βpca)=αaer≥αpca\textnormal{MCorrPCA}\mathopen{}(\mathcal{G},\beta_{\textrm{pca}})=\alpha_{\mathrm{aer}}\geq\alpha_{\textrm{pca}}.

Using (21) also allows us to design a compression block TruncPCA(𝒢,αpca)\textnormal{TruncPCA}\mathopen{}(\mathcal{G},\alpha_{\textrm{pca}}), which, given inputs

  • •

    a set of pp-dimensional vectors 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and

  • •

    a threshold αpca∈(0,1]\alpha_{\textrm{pca}}\in(0,1],

returns

  • •

    the truncated Qr=Q:,1:r∈ℝp×rQ_{r}=Q_{:,1:r}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times r}, and

  • •

where rr is selected as the smallest integer such that MCorrPCA(𝒢,βpca)≥αpca\textnormal{MCorrPCA}\mathopen{}(\mathcal{G},\beta_{\textrm{pca}})\geq\alpha_{\textrm{pca}}. Note that r=0r=0 is possible if the mean value contains enough energy. Using the mean vector 𝝁{\bm{\mu}} and QrQ_{r}, a client can compress a model update slice 𝒈k,i(t){\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t)} by applying (10), and the server decompresses it using (11).

We introduce PCAFed in Algorithm 2, an adaptive compression design that actively measures and exploits the three types of correlation. Each client kk has a state sks_{k}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, that determines the compression mode it currently uses. Every TuT_{u} iterations, the algorithm sets all clients to the update state sk=UPDATEs_{k}=\textnormal{UPDATE}, k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K, to measure the degree of correlation and apply the most suitable compression mode for the subsequent Tu−1T_{u}-1 iterations.

Let PCAFedStateUpdate({𝒈k(t)}k=1,…,K,αPF,βPF)\textnormal{PCAFedStateUpdate}\mathopen{}(\{{\bm{g}}_{k}^{(t)}\}_{k=1,\dots,K},\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}},\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}) be the mechanism that the PSuses to update the compression mode for all clients, where αPF∈[0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}\in[0,1] and βPF∈[0,1]\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\in[0,1]. To do so, the PSmeasures correlation according to the flowchart in Figure 2 to decide the next state of each client. In the absence of temporal correlation, the update mechanism sets sk=LocalPCAs_{k}=\textnormal{LocalPCA}, which requires no additional computations at the PS. A client in this state applies PCA-based compression to its local model update each iteration if sufficient structural correlation is measured within the update. In the presence of temporal correlation, the update method can exploit structural and/or spatial correlation, which correspond to the four cases that use sk=PCAs_{k}=\textnormal{PCA} in Figure 2. In all four cases, the PScomputes the mean 𝝁k,i(t){\bm{\mu}}_{k,i}^{(t)} and the basis matrix Qk,i(t)Q_{k,i}^{(t)}, but each case uses different information depending on the present correlation(s):

  • •

    Spatial and structural correlation:
    Collect nn model update slices from KK clients in hh iterations. Compute one PCAto obtain 𝝁(t),Q(t)=TruncPCA({𝒈k,i(t−t′)}i∈[n],t′∈[h],k∈[K],αPF){\bm{\mu}}^{(t)},Q^{(t)}=\textnormal{TruncPCA}\mathopen{}(\{{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{i\in[n],t^{\prime}\in[h],k\in[K]},\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}), and assign 𝝁k,i(t)=𝝁(t),Qk,i(t)=Q(t),∀i∈[n],∀k∈[K]{\bm{\mu}}_{k,i}^{(t)}={\bm{\mu}}^{(t)},Q_{k,i}^{(t)}=Q^{(t)},\forall i\in[n],\forall k\in[K].

  • •

    Spatial correlation:
    Collect one model update slice from KK clients in hh iterations. Compute nn PCAs(one for each slice) to obtain 𝝁i(t),Qi(t)=TruncPCA({𝒈k,i(t−t′)}t′∈[h],k∈[K],αPF),∀i∈[n]{\bm{\mu}}_{i}^{(t)},Q_{i}^{(t)}=\textnormal{TruncPCA}\mathopen{}(\{{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{t^{\prime}\in[h],k\in[K]},\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}),\forall i\in[n], and assign 𝝁k,i(t)=𝝁i(t),Qk,i(t)=Qi(t),∀i∈[n],∀k∈[K]{\bm{\mu}}_{k,i}^{(t)}={\bm{\mu}}_{i}^{(t)},Q_{k,i}^{(t)}=Q_{i}^{(t)},\forall i\in[n],\forall k\in[K].

  • •

    Structural correlation:
    Collect nn model update slices from one client in hh iterations. Compute KK PCAs(one for each client) to obtain 𝝁k(t),Qk(t)=TruncPCA({𝒈k,i(t−t′)}i∈[n],t′∈[h],αPF){\bm{\mu}}_{k}^{(t)},Q_{k}^{(t)}=\textnormal{TruncPCA}\mathopen{}(\{{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{i\in[n],t^{\prime}\in[h]},\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}), ∀k∈[K]\forall k\in[K], and assign 𝝁k,i(t)=𝝁k(t),Qk,i(t)=Qk(t),∀i∈[n],∀k∈[K]{\bm{\mu}}_{k,i}^{(t)}={\bm{\mu}}_{k}^{(t)},Q_{k,i}^{(t)}=Q_{k}^{(t)},\forall i\in[n],\forall k\in[K].

  • •

    Only temporal correlation:
    Collect one model update slice from one client in hh iterations. Compute n​KnK PCAsto obtain 𝝁k,i(t),Qk,i(t)=TruncPCA({𝒈k,i(t−t′)}t′∈[h],αPF),∀i∈[n],∀k∈[K]{\bm{\mu}}_{k,i}^{(t)},\ Q_{k,i}^{(t)}=\textnormal{TruncPCA}\mathopen{}(\{{\bm{g}}_{k,i}^{(t-t^{\prime})}\}_{t^{\prime}\in[h]},\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}),\forall i\in[n],\allowbreak\forall\penalty{}k\penalty{}\in\penalty{}[K].

The PSthen transmits the corresponding mean vector(s) and basis matrix (matrices) to each client kk with sk=PCAs_{k}=\textnormal{PCA}.

Remark VII.1.

One drawback of this algorithm is the high computational complexity. While impractical in any real implementation, it serves as an example to illustrate how correlation-awareness can be incorporated into the compression design.

VIII Numerical Experiments

In this section, we present simulation results to quantify the degrees of structural, temporal, and spatial correlations, using the metrics discussed in the previous sections.33 3 The code will be publicly available after the review process. We consider three learning tasks with different learning models:

  • •

    A binary classification task, using a linear model fitted via logistic regression. Each data sample (𝝃i,yi)∈ℝd×{−1,1}({\bm{\xi}}_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{-1,1\} is a feature-label pair, and the sample-wise loss ℓ⁡(𝒙,(𝝃i,yi))=log⁡(1+e−yi​𝝃i𝖳​𝒙)\ell({\bm{x}};({\bm{\xi}}_{i},y_{i}))=\log(1+e^{-y_{i}{\bm{\xi}}_{i}^{\mkern-1.5mu\mathsf{T}}{\bm{x}}}). We use the w8a dataset from [7], which contains 49 74949\,749 samples with d=300d=300 features.

  • •

    An image classification task on the MNIST dataset [25], which has 50 00050\,000 training samples, using a small convolutional neural network LeNet [24], with 44 42644\,426 trainable parameters.

  • •

    An image classification task on the CIFAR10 dataset [23], which has 50 00050\,000 training samples, using a larger convolutional neural network ResNet18 [18], with 11 181 64211\,181\,642 trainable parameters.

The training data samples are evenly distributed among the clients in the system. We examine both IID settings, in which each client possesses an equal share of all class labels, and non-IID settings, where clients hold a subset of available classes. Each client applies mini-batch stochastic gradient decent (SGD)and adapts the batch size |𝒟k(t,i)||\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(t,i)}| based on the number of local SGDsteps τ\tau such that |𝒟k(t,i)|⋅τ=|𝒟k||\mathcal{D}_{k}^{(t,i)}|\cdot\tau=|\mathcal{D}_{k}|. For the image classification tasks, we apply heavy-ball momentum with parameter 0.90.9 in the local SGDsteps, and a weight decay of factor 10−410^{-4}.

For learning models whose parameters naturally divide into layers, e.g., the layers of a neural network, we apply compression independently to each such layer. To identify where the largest gains can be achieved by introducing redundancy-based compression, we focus on layers that account for a significant portion of the total parameters. For the LeNet model trained on the MNIST dataset, we consider the fully connected layer fc1, with shape [256,120][256,120], as it contains approximately 70% of the model’s parameters. For the ResNet18 model trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset, we focus on the convolutional layers layer4.0.conv1, with shape [256,512,3,3][256,512,3,3], and layer4.0.conv2, with shape [512,512,3,3][512,512,3,3], which account for approximately 11% and 21% of the total parameters, respectively.

VIII-A Correlation Evolution

Figure 5 shows how the correlation strength evolves during training with K=20K=20 clients. The results indicate that the correlation varies over time and depends on both the model architecture and the data distribution. In Figure 5(a), we see that after an initial phase with high correlation, the IID scenario experiences a substantial decline in spatial correlation and a minor drop in temporal correlation during the later part of training. While initially weaker, the non-IID setting maintains a more stable spatial correlation. Meanwhile, Figure 5(b) shows that the structural correlation is strong regardless of data distribution, while the degree of temporal and spatial correlation is larger in the non-IID setting.

VIII-B Impact of Parameter Reshaping on Structural Correlation

The structural correlation measures in Figure 5 are for one specific mapping from convolutional kernel to model update matrix, that is, n=O​Hn=OH and m=I​Wm=IW.

In Figure 4, we explore different mappings—choosing mm and nn as various combinations of OO, II, HH, and WW—and compare how the MSEof the low-rank approximation G^(t)\widehat{G}^{(t)} reconstructed at the PSvaries with the number of transmitted elements. We present four convolutional layers from different depths in the ResNet18 model: layer1.1.conv2 (5th layer), layer2.1.conv2 (9th layer), layer3.1.conv2 (13th layer), and layer4.1.conv2 (17th layer), in Figures 4(a), 4(b), 4(c) and 4(d), respectively. We find that no single mapping is optimal across all layers, assigning II and OO to different axes generally yields a lower MSEfor the same number of transmitted elements.

VIII-C Impact of Multiple Local Steps on Temporal Correlation

We use cosine similarity to measure the strength of temporal correlation at a single client when using different numbers of local SGDsteps across three learning tasks. For the linear model in (Figure 6(a)), a high degree of temporal correlation is observed for both small (τ=1\tau=1) and large (τ=32\tau=32) numbers of local steps. From Figure 6(b), we observe strong temporal correlation during two distinct phases of the LeNet training process. However, for ResNet18 (Figures 6(c) and 6(d)), the correlation diminishes as the number of local steps increases. These results suggest that the model update trajectory can be more complex for certain models and datasets, resulting in weaker temporal correlation.

VIII-D State Evolution

In Figure 7, we illustrate how the system switches between different states and compression modes when implementing Algorithms 1 and 2. When training LeNet under an IID data distribution, we find that in the early iterations, both AdaSVDFed and PCAFed tend to select compression modes that exploit multiple sources of correlation (e.g., spatial+temporal or spatial+temporal+structural). In the non-IID case, both algorithms use compression modes less frequently that rely less on spatial correlation. However, for ResNet18, the state selection is hindered by the weaker temporal correlation seen in Figures 5(b) and 6, especially for the IID case, which limits how often both algorithms can exploit multiple correlations simultaneously. For AdaSVDFed in Figure 7(c), the results reveal heavy use of the predictive coding mode, where a prediction and a compressed residual are transmitted. For PCAFed in Figure 7(d), the results indicate that LocalPCA is used most frequently, where raw model updates are transmitted due to a lack of correlation. In contrast, the slightly stronger temporal correlation in the non-IID scenario is sufficient to enable joint exploitation of spatial and temporal correlations. In the early iterations in Figure 5(b), we see a spike in temporal correlation, which is believed to cause the temporary use of temporal correlation in Figure 7(d).

VIII-E End-to-End Training Performance of Context-Aware Adaptive Compression Design

At last, we compare the training performance of Algorithms 2 and 1 to a baseline without compression and SVDFed.44 4 we consider a simplified version of SVDFed with periodic updating of the subspace-defining matrix. We apply per-layer compression, and fix the update frequency Tu=3T_{u}=3. For AdaSVDFed, we use h=5h=5, αSF=0.8\alpha_{\mathrm{SF}}=0.8, βSF=0.2\beta_{\mathrm{SF}}=0.2, and let 𝒞(⋅)\mathcal{C}\mathopen{}(\cdot) be a Top-​5%\text{Top-}5\% compression operator, i.e., preserving the 5%5\% elements with largest magnitude (rounded up to the nearest integer). For PCAFed, we use h=5h=5, αPF=0.8\alpha_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.8 and βPF=0.2\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.2. We note that the parameters have not been fine-tuned and may not be optimal for performance. Finding optimal parameters for the compression schemes is outside the scope of this paper and is left for future work.

Generally, we see in Table II that all compression schemes reduce the number of elements in the client-to-PSlinks, at the cost of transmitting more elements in the PS-to-client direction. In some cases, the PS-to-client transmission accounts for the majority of the total communication cost.

The PCAFed scheme shows strong performance on the tasks at hand, and its savings relative to other schemes can be attributed to its ability to adapt to changing correlations during training. In the scenario with stronger correlations (i.e., when training LeNet), we observe comparable iteration complexity. For the larger model (i.e., ResNet18), the iteration complexity increases slightly, but the increase is less pronounced than for the other schemes.

Comparing the number of transmitted elements between SVDFed and AdaSVDFed demonstrates the potential benefit of adaptive designs: in all cases where spatial correlation is weak, we observe a significant reduction in the number of communicated elements in the PS-to-client link. We also observe a significant increase in iteration complexity for SVDFed when temporal correlation is weak, e.g., when training ResNet18.

IX Conclusion and Future Work

We categorize three types of correlation: structural, temporal, and spatial, which are inherent in FLalgorithms. Using unified terminology and notations, we also describe several correlation-exploiting schemes for compressing local model updates in the literature and clarify their underlying design principles. We present numerical examples demonstrating that significant correlations can emerge in certain scenarios and can be leveraged to develop more efficient compression designs. These correlations vary across learning tasks and among different components (e.g., layers of a neural network) of the learned model. Therefore, it is necessary to measure the degree of correlation (either locally or centrally) and adapt compression strategies to the correlation structures of the model components.

We design two adaptive compression algorithms that dynamically switch between different correlation-exploiting modes: one that augments an existing design with a dynamic switching mechanism, and another that can jointly exploit structural, temporal, and spatial correlations when present. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that these adaptive algorithms outperform their non-adaptive counterparts in terms of communication cost. We leave the search for optimal hyperparameters and the further development of optimized, scalable, and correlation-centric designs for future work.

Several other aspects remain to be investigated further, such as considering compression optimized for metrics other than MSE, exploring connections between commonly used bounds and our correlation measurement, and examining the effects of additional algorithmic add-ons (e.g., error compensation).
